title: Firecracker Prices May Jump 30–50% This Diwali as Unsold Stock Piles Up
excerpt: Business Standard’s estimate is steeper than the 15–20% reported earlier this month; in Sivakasi, production at reporting units is down about 25% amid a severe worker shortage.
body:
• Firecracker prices are likely to jump 30–50% this Diwali, Business Standard reported — a steeper estimate than the 15–20% rise reported earlier this month.
  • On the ground in Sivakasi, an ANI report from late September found production at one unit down 25% on last year, with 70–75 workers where 100–120 used to work.
  • Workers and managers cite the worker shortage, green-cracker rules and burst-time restrictions as the squeeze on supply.
  • Orders are lower than last year even from northern India, the unit's manager said — so high prices may meet thin demand.

Firecracker prices are likely to jump 30–50% this Diwali, pinching consumers, Business Standard reported on Thursday — a markedly steeper estimate than the 15–20% rise we reported on October 13, when Sivakasi's production cuts and labour shortage were already pushing prices up. Business Standard's figure is a market estimate ahead of the festival; what is already measurable is what has happened inside Sivakasi's factories.

Inside a Sivakasi Unit

An ANI report from Sivakasi in late September — the ground reporting behind this season's price story — found production at one fireworks unit down 25% compared with last year. The unit now works with 70–75 people where it once employed 100 to 120, its manager Kannan, who has worked there ten years, told ANI, describing a huge worker shortage made worse as more factories open nearby and compete for the same hands.

The unit makes the Diwali staples — flower pots, ground wheels, fancy items, and multi-shot and single-shot fireworks. Orders are coming in from northern India but are lower overall than last year, the manager said.

Why Supply Keeps Shrinking

Workers at the unit pointed to regulation as the other half of the squeeze. Muthulakshmi, who has worked in the industry for 22 years, and colleagues Nagraj and Murugeswari told ANI that the shift to green crackers and restrictions on bursting times have cut production and work, in an industry that is the only local livelihood for many families. Fewer workers, tighter rules and a shorter legal selling window add up to the same arithmetic at retail: less stock chasing the same five days of demand.

What Buyers Should Expect

For families buying this week, the honest summary is a range, not a single number: trade estimates now run as high as the 30–50% Business Standard reported, against a verified production drop of about a quarter in Sivakasi and a workforce down by a third at reporting units. Whether the full estimate shows up on price tags will be decided in the final weekend of sales — and by how much of the northern demand, already softer this year, actually arrives.
nri_angle: Diwali budgets in India — often funded by remittances from the diaspora — face a 30–50% wholesale jump on crackers this year.
author: Diaspora Desk
